steps.title: Stranded by a Thorn
steps.story: Ade, 15, helps out at a busy bike repair workshop. Every week, riders push in bikes with flat tyres: one thorn or one bit of glass, and they're stuck far from home. Some mountain bikers already use a liquid sealant inside their tyres that plugs small holes all by itself. How does it work, and can you make one? Your mission: make a balloon that keeps its air after a pin prick, and measure how many minutes it stays up.

steps.prompt: Do you already have an idea for a tyre that could fix its own hole?

steps.intro: How does nature repair itself? Living things get cut, pricked and torn all the time, and they don't wait for a mechanic. See how they carry their own repair kit!

clues.text: When a rubber tree's bark is cut, milky latex flows into the wound. In the air, the tiny latex particles clump together into a rubbery plug that seals the cut. The natural rubber in many tyres comes from this same latex.

When you cut your skin, blood flows into the gap and tiny cells called platelets clump together at the wound. Threads of a protein called fibrin form a mesh, and a small cut usually stops bleeding within a few minutes.

Mussels anchor to wave-battered rocks with tough threads that stick even underwater. If a thread is stretched too far, special bonds inside it break, then slowly join up again, so the thread heals itself.
When a pine tree is wounded, sticky resin oozes out and covers the damage. As it meets the air, part of it evaporates and it hardens into a seal that keeps insects and fungi out.

steps.secret: Carry the repair kit inside. Each hero stores a liquid that flows to the damage by itself, then clumps or hardens to plug the gap. Pressure helps: blood, latex and resin are pushed towards the hole. Tubeless bike tyres copy this with a latex sealant full of tiny particles. When a thorn makes a hole, the air pressure pushes sealant into it, the particles jam the gap, and the latex dries into a plug. It can seal holes up to about 6 mm. In 2001, scientists at the University of Illinois made a plastic packed with tiny capsules of healing liquid that burst and glue a crack shut. The trade-off: sealant adds weight and slowly dries out, so riders top it up every few months.
steps.reveal_hint: When you get a small cut, where does the fix come from, and what pushes it to the right place?

steps.instructions: Find out which liquid seals a hole best. With an adult, make one pin hole in the bottom of each of 4 identical plastic cups. Hold each cup over a tray and pour in 50 ml of a different test liquid: plain water (your control), water with 1 teaspoon of cornflour, water with a pinch of cotton fluff, and runny PVA glue mixed with cotton fluff. Count the drips in 1 minute for each cup and record them in a table.
hints: Change only the liquid. Same cup, same size hole, same amount of liquid, same height above the tray.
Particles help: cornflour and fibres get pulled into the hole by the flowing liquid and jam it, just like platelets in a cut. Fibres plus a glue that dries usually seal best.

steps.prompt: Draw your self-healing balloon as two cross-sections: before and after the prick.
steps.guidance: Show where the sealant sits, where the pin goes in, and arrows for how air pressure pushes sealant into the hole. Label what jams the hole and what hardens it.

steps.instructions: Make self-healing balloons. Use a funnel to put 2 teaspoons of your best sealant inside a balloon, blow it up, tie it and swirl it so the inside is coated. Stick a small square of clear tape on the outside where it will be pricked: like a scab, it stops the rubber tearing. An adult pricks each balloon through the tape with a pin and pulls the pin out. Time how many minutes the balloon stays up, until it has shrunk to about half its size. Test a balloon with tape but no sealant as your control. Work over a tray and wear safety glasses in case one pops. Skip this test if anyone has a latex allergy.
test_criteria: How many minutes did each balloon stay up after the prick? Record the sealant balloon and the tape-only control in a table.
Repeat each test 3 times and work out the average: one balloon can be lucky.
Look at the prick: can you see a little plug or crust where the sealant filled the hole?
Improve one thing and test again. Change the amount of sealant or the particles, and compare the minutes.
hints: If the balloon pops straight away, the rubber is tearing, not leaking. Add a second layer of tape, and prick near the knot or the dark spot at the top, where the rubber is thicker and less stretched.

Make sure the sealant is sitting on the prick spot: hold the balloon so the liquid pools under the tape before the adult pricks it. Glue, water and fibres together usually seal far better than a plain liquid.

steps.celebration_text: Pssst… then silence! Your balloon healed itself, just like a rubber tree seals its bark. Ade's workshop wants to try your sealant idea in a real inner tube.
steps.share_prompt: Share a photo of your balloons and your minutes table on the Ideas Wall. Which nature trick did your sealant copy, and what did your I Like, I Wish, What If feedback say?

age_tier_variants.summary: Compare sealant recipes in a controlled leak test, build a self-sealing balloon, average repeated trials, and relate latex, blood clotting and microcapsule self-healing plastics to tubeless tyre design and its trade-offs.
